cause.statement: A force epoch is carried in one double Julian date, and the two-term TDB-TT approximation is quantized in that representation before its inverse enters Earth rotation. At the worst rotation epoch the signed force-clock error plus ERFA TDB-TT minus the quantized inverse correction is 14.201 us, giving 0.213601 mas at Earth rotation rate; the measured reference rotation is 0.213831 mas (0.000230 mas numerical rotation-evaluation residual). The 46.134 us maximum force-clock error occurs at a different epoch and must not be added as an unsigned maximum. The clock and interpolated pole together bound LEO displacement by 7.043 mm. This measured rotation angle sets the achievable tolerance; the original 0.022 mas limit remains a miss.

evidence.toleranceRationale: The original limit only budgets the 0.02 mas pole interpolation plus small rounding; its implied time budget is in precision.allowedTimeErrorAt022MasS. It does not cover single-JD Earth rotation.

cause.statement: The J2000-to-date function substitutes T for the initial-epoch t0 in the general-epoch IAU 1976 coefficients. For J2000, t0 must be zero. Evaluating both formulae reproduces the 206 mas error; this is not an IAU 1976-versus-2006 reference spread.

rows.note: The 63-row table has 62 ERFA argument keys, ten coefficient mismatches and one spurious key. There are 44 omitted ERFA terms, including a 4.8 mas longitude coefficient. See the measured cause; the historical truncation note is retained separately.

cause.statement: The 49 mas discrepancy is caused chiefly by erroneous retained coefficient assignments, not precession contamination or eps0. The 63 FFM rows contain only 62 ERFA argument keys, ten coefficient mismatches and one spurious key; 44 ERFA terms are absent, including a 4.8 mas longitude coefficient. Thus the historical note claiming 43 omissions all below 0.3 mas is incorrect. At the worst epoch, replacing the coefficients changes the matrix by 43.506 mas and restoring omitted terms by 5.582 mas; these rotations combine vectorially to the measured 49.083 mas.

rows.historicalNote: FFM keeps 63 of the 106 terms (each omitted term under 0.3 mas)

rows.note: the plugin's coords::transform TEME axes

cause.statement: The plugin coords TEME chain inherits the erroneous precession and nutation coefficients. Holding the epoch fixed and correcting precession alone reduces the maximum to 19.586 mas. Correcting nutation everywhere, including its equation-of-equinoxes contribution, leaves 1.196 mas from the simplified equation of equinoxes; using eraEqeq94 leaves numerical roundoff. The separate SGP4/foundation TEME chain passes and does not use this function.

cause.statement: The fallback inherits the same precession and nutation-table defects through N*P. A C++ reconstruction with the same one-hour cache reproduces the stored result to 0.0031 mas (large-angle GMST/compiler arithmetic); correcting P, N and the equation of equinoxes leaves 5.910 mas, including the cache and the single-JD sidereal clock. The original 211.890 mas miss remains recorded.

verdict.statement: The table retains all original scores and limits. Six of 23 rows miss stated limits: four expose two FFM classical-frame defects, one exposes the single-JD clock precision, and one exceeds a limit smaller than the measured reference spread. Untoleranced rows are diagnostic comparisons, not passes.

e2e.replay: Rebuild pinned C++ ERFA and foundation/frames offline, evaluate 50 epochs, compare with independently stored reference matrices, and re-score the original pinned matrices.
e2e.toleranceRationale: Original stored-matrix reduction differs only by the final hypot rounding; fresh native compilation can differ by tiny matrix-element contraction/rounding differences. Rebuilding both sides permits 1e-8 mas for C++ versus historical NumPy matrix rounding. These numerical replay tolerances are far below the original 0.001 mas physical limit.
